analysis.one_liner: Bans contracts that require workers to pay union dues or fees as a condition of employment.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 22 Republican cosponsors but never got a hearing, a vote, or any action in the Senate Labor Committee, and died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend federal labor law to outlaw 'union security' agreements nationwide, in both private industry and railroads. Under such agreements, a union that wins an election and bargains for a workplace can require every employee to join the union or pay fees for the representation it provides. The bill would strike those provisions from the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act, making it illegal for any employer to require union dues or fees as a condition of employment.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who oppose unions or do not want to pay dues or fees would keep the full benefit of union-negotiated contracts without paying for them. Employers would also gain: unions depend on dues and fees for revenue, so eliminating mandatory fees shrinks union treasuries and weakens their leverage in bargaining and in politics.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the National Labor Relations Act to repeal the provisions that let a collective bargaining agreement require employees to join a union or pay dues and fees as a condition of employment, including the clause that permits employers to fire workers who do not pay.
It repeals the parallel provision in the Railway Labor Act, ending the ability of railroad carriers to require union dues payroll deduction as a condition of employment.

After enactment, no private-sector employee anywhere in the country could be legally required to financially support a union, extending right-to-work rules that about half of states had adopted on their own to all fifty states.

analysis.who_pays: Unions that represent covered workers lose the ability to collect fees from the employees they are legally required to represent, cutting their revenue. That money is what funds contract negotiations, grievance handling, and organizing. Workers covered by union contracts may see weaker contracts over time as unions are squeezed, because everyone covered by a union contract receives its benefits whether they pay or not — the same 'free rider' dynamic that has been observed in right-to-work states, where research finds lower wages and less union representation.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the fees that fund union representation while leaving unions legally obligated to represent every employee under a union contract, so a union must spend money bargaining and grieving for workers who pay nothing toward it.

Eliminating union-security agreements nationwide would reduce union revenue and membership over time; states with right-to-work laws have historically had lower wages and lower union density, and the same mechanism would apply nationally.
Workers who value the union contract and want to fund it would be barred from doing so through an agreed dues requirement, even if the union and a majority of the workforce voted for one.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters honestly argue that no worker should be forced to fund a private organization to keep a job, and individual workers who object to unions do keep more of their paycheck. But the bill's design removes the funding for union bargaining without removing unions' legal duty to bargain for everyone, which shifts bargaining power toward employers. The concentrated beneficiaries are employers and the political opponents of unions; the cost is spread diffusely across union-represented workers' contracts and wages.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken on it before the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jim DeMint introduced the National Right-to-Work Act in the Senate on March 8, 2011, with seven original cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
Twenty-two Republicans ultimately cosponsored the bill, all of them Republicans.
The committee took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Labor unions and workers who depend on union bargaining are better off because the bill died, and the employers who would have gained a permanent national right-to-work rule never got it.

for.name: Sen. Jim DeMint
for.role: U.S. Senator from South Carolina (bill sponsor)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Right-to-Work Act and recruited original cosponsors including Sens. Coburn, Hatch, Lee, Paul, Toomey, Vitter, and Risch.

against.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; the committee record shows no action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill; the Democratic committee chair allowed it no committee action.

industries.note: Unions would lose mandatory dues and fees that fund contract negotiation and grievance representation, shrinking their capacity to bargain on behalf of workers. Their interest runs alongside the workers who rely on union contracts.

Employers would face unions with less revenue and less member commitment, giving them more leverage in bargaining. Their gain comes at the expense of the workers whose contracts would be weakened over time.
